Platitude

PLAT-ih-tood · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Platitude is a stale, overused remark that sounds wise but says nothing new.

Instead of any real advice, the motivational poster just offered the tired platitude that 'every cloud has a silver lining.'

Worked Example

The graduation speaker leaned on the same platitude about following your dreams that every speaker before him had already used.

The line sounded wise on the surface, but because it was so overused and generic, it didn't actually tell the graduates anything new -- exactly what makes it a platitude.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cliche: an overused expression or idea

truism: a statement so obviously true it hardly needs saying

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

insight: a fresh, genuinely useful understanding

Where it sits · how far hollow talk poses as wisdom — generic comment → platitude → empty rhetoric

generic comment vs. platitude: A generic comment is simply vague; a platitude goes further, presenting itself as if it were wise or comforting.

empty rhetoric vs. platitude: Empty rhetoric goes even further than a single platitude, describing an entire speech built from nothing but hollow, feel-good lines.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Platitude traces to French plat, 'flat,' plus the noun-forming suffix -itude ('state of being') -- literally the 'state of being flat,' fitting for a remark with no depth to it.

Use the root in a new word: plateau

Use the root in a new word: plateau: Plateau also comes from French plat, 'flat' -- a flat stretch of high ground, the same root imagined in landscape rather than language.
